transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Mark Chen (Aurora Head of Platform), Priya Nair (Aurora ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Aurora SRE), Nina Patel (Aurora PM)

Summary:
Quick sync on POC latency results this week. Focus: TTFT (time-to-first-token), streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, sequence length distribution impact, and kernel/quant choices for stable P99. Agreed actions around kernel tuning, dedicated test nodes, and next benchmark run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sara Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, appreciate it. quick agenda — diego will run through results, then we chat tuning and next steps.
[00:15] Diego Alvarez: Cool, thanks Sara. So we ran three config sets this week: hosted baseline, streaming enabled with chunked tokens, and dedicated int8 profile on the dedicated nodes. I have slides but i'll share the spreadsheet after.
[00:42] Mark Chen: quick clarification — the dedicated nodes you used, are they the same GPU type we talked about? (i think they were A10s?)
[00:55] Diego Alvarez: Yeah sorry i said A10G in the notes but the cluster used A100S — mismatch in the doc, my bad. performance numbers reflect A100S.
[01:10] Priya Nair: ok that explains the jump in throughput we saw, can you call out TTFT numbers? we care a lot about that for the customer flow.
[01:22] Diego Alvarez: Sure — TTFT for baseline hosted was about 180ms median, 420ms p95, p99 around 920ms. Streaming reduced median to 120ms and p95 to around 360ms, p99 improved to ~800ms. The int8 dedicated run gave best average token throughput but slightly worse p99 in some cases — we think kernel selection and sequence length mismatch caused micro spikes.
[01:52] Liam O'Connor: When you say "streaming" are you chunking at 64 tokens? what's the chunking config?
[02:03] Diego Alvarez: We tested 64 and 128 token chunk sizes. 64 gave fastest TTFT but slightly higher overall token cost. 128 smoothed bursts and improved P99 for long sequences.
[02:22] Nina Patel: our profile is lots of short messages — ~60% under 80 tokens, but 10% are 400-600 tokens for batch compliance checks. that tail is the issue.
[02:39] Diego Alvarez: That's helpful. The long tail is where KV cache and kernel selection matter. On A100S we saw the int8 kernel path optimized for 512 sequence length — for 600 tokens it falls back to a slower kernel.
[02:56] Mark Chen: is the fallback deterministic? can we force a different kernel or quant profile for long sequences?
[03:08] Diego Alvarez: You can pin kernel choices in our runtime config per route. Two levers: prefer int8 for 512 and below, or use fp16 path for above-512 sequences. Pinning fp16 for long sequences gave more consistent p99 but cost went up ~20%.
[03:30] Priya Nair: what's the impact on TTFT when switching to fp16 for long sequences?
[03:36] Diego Alvarez: TTFT median stayed similar, but p95/p99 for those long requests improved — the spikes reduced because the slower fallback disappeared.
[03:48] Sara Kim: quick commercial note — we can include a hybrid route in the pilot so long sequences hit dedicated fp16 pool and short ones hit int8 optimized pool.
[04:02] Mark Chen: that sounds good. Security question — do you log full request payloads in the debug traces? our security team will be picky.
[04:12] Diego Alvarez: We do optional request-level tracing but payload capture toggles are off by default for the pilot. We can provide redacted traces and of course we have KMS integration and SOC2 docs. I'll send the network diagram.
[04:29] Liam O'Connor: also need the IP list for the test endpoints to open firewall rules.
[04:33] Sara Kim: noted, will include IPs in the follow-up.
[04:40] Diego Alvarez: Back to the tuning — we tried a kernel mix that pins 512 int8 and forces a different launch config for 600+ tokens; latency improved but throughput dropped for medium-length requests. It's a tradeoff.
[05:02] Priya Nair: can you quantify throughput drop? We need baseline QPS numbers to weigh tradeoffs.
[05:10] Diego Alvarez: Roughly a 12-15% throughput drop at 200 concurrent streams when forcing fp16 on long tails. At 50 concurrent it's negligible.
[05:22] Mark Chen: So for our expected peak — around 120 concurrent — it's gonna bite us a bit. Is there an adaptive policy?
[05:30] Diego Alvarez: Yes — we can set a routing policy: if estimated seq_len > 512 route to fp16 pool; OR by latency budget: if request's latency SLO is strict route to low-latency pool. We can also do on-the-fly fallback thresholds.
[05:46] Nina Patel: does Redwood's runtime expose hooks for us to set those thresholds via API?
[05:51] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, config API supports per-route thresholds and dynamic weight changes. we'll share example configs.
[06:00] Mark Chen: on the streaming side — any artifacts on reassembly cost on client side? we must ensure client latency doesn't spike because of chunking.
[06:10] Diego Alvarez: Good point. Streaming reduces server TTFT but client-side reassembly cost depends on your client stack. For web it was fine; for some of your older microservices you'll need to ensure they process partial frames.
[06:25] Priya Nair: we can test with our Java client, i'll add that to the test matrix.
[06:30] Diego Alvarez: Great. Next item was kernel selection heuristics — we found the runtime can pick a suboptimal kernel when seq distribution is bimodal, so manual overrides helped.
[06:43] Sara Kim: Diego, do you have recommended defaults we should push into the pilot?
[06:48] Diego Alvarez: For Aurora profile i'd recommend: streaming enabled with 64-token chunks for <128 requests; dynamic routing to fp16 dedicated pool for estimated seq_len >512; int8 default for 128-512; aggressive KV cache for repeated prefixes.
[07:06] Mark Chen: aggressive KV cache — any memory implications?
[07:10] Diego Alvarez: Yes, KV cache uses GPU memory; we can size caches per model instance. For A100S it's fine but on smaller GPUs you'll need to trim or shard the cache.
[07:22] Liam O'Connor: can the cache be sharded across pods to avoid OOM?
[07:27] Diego Alvarez: We support sharded KV across worker pools, yes. We'll include recommended cache sizes in the spreadsheet.
[07:36] Nina Patel: Question on monitoring — we need token-level cost and latency dashboards for each route. Do you have that out of the box?
[07:45] Sara Kim: Yes Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdown and per-route latency histograms. We can give a sample dashboard.
[07:53] Priya Nair: any chance to run a 10k concurrent token stream to reproduce a particular spike we saw?
[07:59] Diego Alvarez: We can run 10k synthetic streams but it'd be short burst testing. For sustained load i'd recommend the dedicated pool.
[08:10] Mark Chen: ok next — can you send the updated pricing if we add the hybrid fp16 pool for tails?
[08:15] Sara Kim: i'll include pricing for hybrid setup in the follow-up along with pilot addendum.
[08:22] Diego Alvarez: i'll log the kernel tuning patch i used and run one more int8/ fp16 comparison targeting 600 token sequences.
[08:30] Priya Nair: i'll upload our sample traffic file to the shared drive after the call.
[08:35] Sara Kim: great — recap of actions then.
[08:40] Diego Alvarez: Action: test kernel mix and share results (Diego, due 2027-01-07).
[08:46] Priya Nair: Action: upload traffic profile (Priya, due 2027-01-06).
[08:50] Liam O'Connor: Action: open firewall for test IPs (Liam).
[08:55] Sara Kim: Action: send pricing and SOC2/network docs (Sara, due 2027-01-08).
[09:05] Mark Chen: sounds good, let's reconvene next week same time.
[09:10] Sara Kim: thanks everyone, bye.

Notes:
- Diego to prioritize a kernel run that forces fp16 for seq > 512 and report p99/TTFT and throughput delta.
- Recommended pilot config: streaming for short messages (64-chunks), int8 for mid-length, fp16 dedicated pool for tails.
- Security follow-ups: SOC2 pack, redacted traces, network diagram, test IPs.

References shared during call:
- benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat)
- Redwood pilot addendum (doc link)

End of transcript.
